solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Horse getting fitter, needing a drink

indicators.note: to be needing something is to be without it, so a letter is missing from the word before

blocks.note: a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse
fitter as in more capable
the letter taken away

explanation.surface: A horse being trained into shape is thirsty and wants a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing a' reads as wanting a drink, but needing means lacking: the capable word goes without its A. The definition is just 'drink', with the surface's 'a' borrowed for the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobbler is an iced cocktail of wine or sherry, sugar and fruit, traditionally sipped through a straw.

clue.text: Talks over, sanctions must be resolved

indicators.note: resolving something breaks it down and settles it afresh, so the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Diplomatic negotiations have ended and the dispute over sanctions now has to be settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talks over' reads as a single phrase meaning negotiations finished, but 'over' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Talks and conversations are both nouns for spoken exchanges between people, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Air strike failing completely

blocks.note: first meaning: an attack by aircraft dropping explosives
second meaning: flopping badly, as a show that dies on stage

explanation.surface: An aerial attack that goes entirely wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a failed raid; really the two phrases are separate senses of one word, the second being informal.
explanation.definitionFit: A raid from planes is a noun sense of the word, while the slang verb means to flop disastrously, as a comedian dying on stage.

clue.text: Strip on edge of mown lawn

indicators.note: an edge is a boundary, and here the trailing boundary of the next word supplies one letter

blocks.note: a line is a narrow strip or stripe
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A gardener's stripe running along the border of a freshly cut lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lawn' looks like grass, but it is also a fine cloth; 'on' in a down clue puts one piece after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn is a very fine, sheer plain-woven fabric, originally made from flax, so it is a type of that cloth.

clue.text: Fat for suet pudding

blocks.note: first meaning: plump and round, an adjective
second meaning: a rolled pudding spread with jam

explanation.surface: Which fat to use in making a suet pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'fat' as a cooking ingredient; it is really the adjective meaning chubby. Jam roly-poly is a traditional British steamed or baked pudding of suet pastry rolled round jam.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a chubby, rounded person and also names the rolled British dessert made with suet pastry.

clue.text: A cat having tail nibbled by mountain creature

indicators.note: a tail bitten off is shortened at the back, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: an alp is a high mountain
taken as written
taken as written before it loses its end

explanation.surface: A cat whose tail has been bitten by some animal living in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountain creature' wants to be the definition, but 'mountain' is ALP, placed by (next to) the other pieces; 'creature' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: An alpaca is a domesticated South American camelid kept for wool, so it is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Nameless person greeting visiting queen

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone else's home, so one piece enters another

blocks.note: yo is an informal hello
Queen Anne, the British monarch

explanation.surface: An unidentified person says hello while calling on a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The queen here is named rather than abbreviated: ANNE, split to take the greeting in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun refers to any unspecified individual, someone not identified by name at all.

clue.text: Criticise Yankee wearing the aforementioned garment

indicators.note: whoever is wearing clothes is covered by them, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: to pan is to review harshly
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet
those things already mentioned

explanation.surface: A critic attacking an American for wearing the clothing just referred to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The aforementioned' is a formal way of saying those things, and the Yankee letter goes inside it just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantyhose is the American word for tights, a sheer legwear item, so it is an example of clothing.

clue.text: Atmosphere around capital city cold and extremely tense

indicators.note: to go around something is to surround it on both sides
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only those letters are kept

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
Lima is the capital of Peru
the first and last letters of the word, its two extremes

explanation.surface: The mood in some capital is chilly and very strained.
explanation.walkthrough: The cold C and the ends of 'tense' go around the capital, one on each side.
explanation.definitionFit: Climate can mean the prevailing mood or conditions, as in a political climate, just as atmosphere does.

clue.text: No small time friend, ostensibly

blocks.note: taken as written
min is the short form of minute, a small unit of time
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Someone who is supposedly a friend but not merely a small-time acquaintance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small time' looks like an adjective meaning minor league; it is a short measure of time, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adverbs describe something true in name or appearance only, not in actual practice or reality.

clue.text: Turning near Scotsman’s place in Highland region

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: NR is the standard abbreviation for near
Ian is a typical Scottish first name

explanation.surface: Directions to a Scotsman's house, turning off near somewhere in the Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Scotsman's' only glues the surface together. Highland is a council area in the far north of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairn is a small seaside town on the Moray Firth east of Inverness, within the Highland council area.

clue.text: Presumably feel obliged to cut speech, of course

definitions.text: Presumably feel obliged to cut speech

blocks.clueFragment: Presumably feel obliged to cut speech
blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: to require fewer words
second meaning: obviously, it goes without mention

explanation.surface: Someone apparently compelled to trim a speech, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the phrase as NEED LESS TO SAY and it describes someone obliged to shorten their remarks; 'presumably' flags that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The set phrase is used when something is obvious and hardly worth mentioning, exactly like 'naturally' or 'obviously'.

clue.text: Rejected natural water source

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: naive as in unaffected, artless

explanation.surface: A spring of natural water has been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natural water' looks like a phrase; 'natural' is the word to turn round and 'water source' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Evian is a French spa town whose springs supply a famous brand of bottled mineral water.

clue.text: Song writer introducing new end to My Way

indicators.note: an end is the final part, so only the closing letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: a pen is a thing that writes
N is the abbreviation for new
the final letter of the word
a lane is a narrow way or road

explanation.surface: A songwriter unveils a fresh ending for Sinatra's 'My Way'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My Way' is the Sinatra song, the obvious red herring; its two words are split, one giving its last letter and the other a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Penny Lane is a 1967 Beatles hit named after a street in Liverpool, so it is an example of a song.

clue.text: Sons getting work in parts of Malaga lopped tree

indicators.note: lopping cuts off an end, so the last letter is removed
to part something is to split it up, so the letters are broken and rearranged
one thing placed within another sits inside it

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for sons
op is short for opus, a musical work
the Spanish city's name, before losing its final letter

explanation.surface: Sons find jobs in parts of Malaga where trees have been cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts of Malaga' looks like districts of the city, but 'parts' is a verb telling you to break up the lopped name, with OP then set inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The sago palm is a tropical palm tree whose pith yields the starch called sago, so it is a kind of tree.

clue.text: To keep going is difficult after exercises, right?

blocks.note: PE is physical education
R is the abbreviation for right
severe as in hard, demanding

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether carrying on after a workout is hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the difficult word behind the exercises-and-right pair; the question mark only serves the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To persevere is to continue steadily despite obstacles, which is what carrying on or not giving up means.

clue.text: Controversial politician in good health after back operation

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: op is short for operation
well means healthy

explanation.surface: A divisive politician is healthy again following surgery on his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back operation' reads as spinal surgery; 'back' actually turns the short form of operation around. Enoch Powell was a British politician notorious for his 1968 'Rivers of Blood' speech on immigration.
explanation.definitionFit: Enoch Powell was a British Conservative and later Ulster Unionist MP whose inflammatory speeches made him deeply divisive.

clue.text: River banks protecting one French city

indicators.note: whatever protects something wraps around it as a shield

blocks.note: the Po is the longest river in Italy
I is the Roman numeral one
banks as in rows or levels, like banks of seats

explanation.surface: The banks of a river shield a single French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' is not riverside but rows, as in banks of seats; the river and the rows together hold the one between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Poitiers is a historic city in west-central France, site of famous battles in 732 and 1356.

clue.text: Teachers make disapproving sound or shout at the front

indicators.note: the front of a word is where it begins, so its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: tut is a click of the tongue showing disapproval
taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Teachers at the front of a class either tut or yell at pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface picture of a teacher at the front of the room hides that 'at the front' takes only the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutors are private or university instructors, so the word is a close synonym for people who teach.

clue.text: Limit that is ultimately enforced in urban area

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is taken
something placed in something else ends up surrounded by it

blocks.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
the final letter of the word
a town is an urban area

explanation.surface: A restriction that is eventually enforced in a city.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation and the final letter go together inside the town, splitting it after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To tie down someone is to restrict their freedom or commit them, so it means to restrict or constrain.

clue.text: Acquisitive old fellow, in our opinion

blocks.note: cove is old British slang for a man or chap
as in 'it seems so to us'

explanation.surface: We think the old man is greedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old fellow' tempts you to use O for old; instead the whole phrase is dated slang for a chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe someone greedy for possessions, eager to get and keep more things, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Borneo’s revolutionary playwright

indicators.note: a revolution turns things over completely, so the letters are overturned into a new order

blocks.note: the island's name with its possessive S

explanation.surface: A dramatist who led an uprising in Borneo.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's supplies a letter, not grammar; 'revolutionary' looks like a description of the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: John Osborne was the English dramatist who wrote Look Back in Anger, so he is an example of a dramatist.

clue.text: Two subjects acceptable in English school

blocks.note: RE (religious education) and PT (physical training), two school subjects
on as in allowed, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: Two subjects that pass muster in the curriculum of an English school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's not on' means unacceptable, so ON can mean acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Repton is a long-established fee-paying boarding school in Derbyshire, England, hence a particular British school.

clue.text: Old audit including King and Queen’s tax

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece holds others

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
to vet is to examine or check
Rex is Latin for king
ER, Elizabeth Regina, with 's as 'is'

explanation.surface: An old accounts check that covers a royal tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax' is a verb, not a levy; the 's after Queen reads as 'is', linking wordplay to definition. Rex is the Latin title a king signs with.
explanation.definitionFit: To tax someone is to strain them heavily, and to overtax or push too hard is exactly the meaning here.

clue.text: Sip beer regularly in teetotal country

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is taken
placed in something means surrounded by it

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
TT means teetotal, abstaining from alcohol

explanation.surface: Drinking beer now and then in a nation where alcohol is banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teetotal' abbreviates to TT, whose two letters surround the regular picks.
explanation.definitionFit: Tibet is a Himalayan region, historically an independent state, commonly treated in crosswords as a land or nation.

clue.text: Aristocrat in Elizabethan era

indicators.note: a word lying in a phrase is contained within its letters, running across the join

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A nobleman living in the time of Queen Elizabeth I.
explanation.walkthrough: The Elizabethan setting fits the word too: Shakespeare's Macbeth is Thane of Cawdor.
explanation.definitionFit: A thane was a man holding land from a king in Anglo-Saxon England or Scotland, a rank of nobleman.

clue.text: Kid tucked into ends of stale cake

indicators.note: tucking something into a space puts it inside
the ends of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: to kid is to fool or con
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A child tucks into the leftover ends of an old cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a child eating; it is the verb meaning to fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A scone is a small British baked item, a plain or fruit teacake served with butter, jam or cream.

clue.text: With nothing to lose, author uses complex reference book

indicators.note: nothing is the letter O, and having it to lose means it is taken away
something complex is intricately put together, so the letters are woven into a new pattern

blocks.note: the two words with the O removed

explanation.surface: A writer with no stake left turns to a complicated reference work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' is O, which the fodder loses before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesaurus lists synonyms and related words, the classic volume consulted by writers, a kind of work you look things up in.

clue.text: Student initially engrossed by article, in French translation

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is taken
to be engrossed by something is to be absorbed into it

blocks.note: une is the French indefinite article
the first letter
en is French for in

explanation.surface: A pupil absorbed by a piece of French writing to be put into English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' serves both the article and 'in': UNE and EN. An unseen is a passage set for translation in an exam without prior preparation.
explanation.definitionFit: In British schools an unseen is a passage given for translation in an exam, one not studied in advance.

clue.text: View endless track followed by European railway

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: a scent is a trail an animal leaves, which hounds track
E is the abbreviation for European
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Admiring an unending line of track that runs on into a Continental railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' is a noun for a trail, as the scent a dog follows, not a rail line.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenery is the landscape seen around one, so it matches a vista or panorama laid out before the eye.
